bio.en: Nickey Skarstad is a product leader at Duolingo (and formerly Airbnb and The Wing) known internally as a PM who gets things done, and a repeated community recommendation as an under-the-radar guest.
bio.zh: 尼基·斯卡斯塔德（Nickey Skarstad）是 Duolingo 的产品负责人（此前在 Airbnb 和 The Wing），以"能把事做成"的 PM 闻名于内部，也是社群反复推荐、却低调的嘉宾。

summary.en: Nickey walks through setting vision, translating it into goals, and executing with alignment, plus how to run effective product review sessions. She shares the skills that powered her rise from forum moderator to director of product. The episode is a grounded playbook for turning strategy into shipped, high-quality product.
summary.zh: 尼基逐步讲解了如何设定愿景、转化为目标并对齐执行，以及如何开好产品评审会。她分享了让自己从论坛版主一路成长为产品总监的本领。本期是一份扎实的手册，关于如何把战略变为已交付、高质量的产品。

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Thank you. Thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢。感谢邀请。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My pleasure. Today, you are director of product at Duolingo, which is an awesome product, and something that I used to use. I'm not learning a language currently, but I know where to go if I were to. Can you just talk about how you got into product, and then a bit about just your journey from that point to where you are today?
turns.zh: 很荣幸。如今，您是多邻国（Duolingo）的产品总监，这个产品太棒了，我以前也用过。虽然我现在没有在学习语言，但如果有需要，我知道该去哪儿找资源。您能谈谈您是如何进入产品领域的，以及从那时到如今的职业发展历程吗？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah, so it's been a long, meandering journey, which is fun. And so I've been in technology roles now for 12 years. I've been in PM roles, actually product roles, for 10. I'm starting to be the person with experience in the room, which is really fun and kind of daunting at times. But how I got my first role in product was I was at Etsy in 2010 is when I joined. And I joined them, I'd say it was post-product market fit, but before they truly started to really grow and scale. And I actually joined them on their community team. So I worked as a forums moderator, and then as a seller education specialist. Yeah. Spent a couple years doing that. And then through that process became sort of one of the internal voices that had a really good understanding of how their customer, one of their core customers, their sellers, were actually using their product. (00:04:38): And the VP product at the time, his name's Mark Headland. Hey Mark, if you're listening. Was like, "Hey, Nickey, you're in all these product meetings. Have you thought about being a product manager?" And at the time I was like, "Oh God, no. Never." I was like, "No. Technology what? Engineering? I'd have to work with engineers? I know nothing about engineering." And so I was very imposter syndrome-y about it. And he gave me a little nudge, and was like, "I think you'd be really good at it." (00:04:59): And so I tried it. And I started as an APM. And I was at Etsy for around, I think, it was seven years total, and spent the majority of time actually in PM product roles. So I left as a director of product. And for most of my time there, I worked on the seller side. So it was all seller tooling, working with sellers to figure out how they could grow and scale their businesses. And it was an awesome, wild ride. But that was my first role in product. And then I went on after that into several other product roles as well.
turns.zh: 是啊，这是一段漫长而曲折的旅程，但也很有趣。到现在，我从事科技行业已经12年了，其中产品经理（PM）岗位做了10年。现在我逐渐成为团队中经验丰富的老手，既兴奋又有些许压力。但我如何踏入产品领域的呢？2010年我加入Etsy时，公司已经过了产品市场验证期，但尚未真正开始大规模扩张。我当时加入的是社区团队，先是担任论坛版主，后来又转任卖家教育专员。就这样工作了几年。在此过程中，我逐渐成为内部专家，深入了解核心客户——卖家群体如何使用产品。（00:04:38）当时的VP产品Mark Headland（Mark，如果你能听到的话）问我：“Nick，你经常参加产品会议，有没有考虑过成为产品经理？”我当时的反应是“天哪，不行！绝对不行！”我觉得自己对工程技术一窍不通，还深受冒名顶替综合症的困扰。但Mark鼓励我：“我觉得你会很出色的。”于是我尝试了一下，以助理产品经理（APM）的身份入职。在Etsy工作了约七年后，大部分时间都担任产品经理职位，最后以产品总监的身份离职。期间我主要专注于卖家业务，致力于帮助他们提升业务规模。这是一段疯狂而精彩的旅程。但这就是我进入产品领域的起点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, let's get into it. Where'd you go next?
turns.zh: 好的，接下来您能讲讲后续的经历吗？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: So after seven years at Etsy, I was kind of getting the itch to try something new. When I took a step back and was like, all right, what do I want to do next? I really loved the marketplace component at Etsy. And I don't know if this is just says something about my personality, or actually probably your personality too, is marketplace product is really hard, right? You have this constant balancing of both buyer and seller sides or both sides of the marketplace. And I really liked that. And it was something that I was good at. (00:05:54): And so I was like, all right, where else could I go that's interesting or having a moment? And I was like, Airbnb. Has to be Airbnb. I was a huge fan of their product. They were also post-product market fit. But sniffed around, ended up basically getting an opportunity to join the experiences team. And I joined that team when the product had just launched. So they had done sort of their early thinking, the existential thinking. Had a brand new product in market, and then I joined the team. (00:06:18): And so I was the first boots on the ground product manager, and really helped that team figure out how do we get product market fit? And then how do we start to think about how to scale it, which was, you can imagine, experiences is interesting because it is a very nuanced product in that, and this is similar to Airbnb if you work on homes as well, but part of it is building the digital experience that someone will interact with when they're booking an Airbnb experience. And the other part is actually influencing the live event experience that you will experience when you actually join an event or an experience. (00:06:52): And I think that layer of abstraction for me was really fascinating, and something I've learned a ton about is it's not just influencing the digital product, but it's actually the consumer experience when their boots around the ground. And that is another layer of complexity. And so that was super fun. I was there for about, I think, a little over two and a half years. Started as a PM. I think I got promoted a couple times. Left as senior product lead, I believe was my title. And forever grateful for that experience because I learned a ton about product market fit and also product quality.
turns.zh:
于是，在Etsy工作了七年后，我开始渴望尝试新事物。当我退后一步，问自己：接下来我想做什么？我真的很喜欢Etsy的市场平台部分。不知道这是否反映了我的性格特质，或许也反映了你的性格特质——市场产品的开发确实充满挑战，对吧？你需要在买家和卖家双方，或者说市场的两端之间不断平衡利益。我很喜欢这种挑战，而且我也擅长处理这类问题。（00:05:54）  
于是我开始思考：还有哪些有趣的公司或领域值得探索？我首先想到Airbnb。必须是Airbnb。我一直是他们产品的忠实用户，而且他们的产品也已经完成了市场验证阶段。但经过一番探索，我最终获得了加入体验团队的机会。当时产品刚刚上线，我加入时他们已经完成了早期构想和存在性验证阶段。产品已经进入市场，但我还是团队中首位实地参与的产品经理。我帮助团队探索如何实现产品与市场的适配，以及如何推动规模化发展。要知道，体验类产品本质上很复杂——如果你也负责Airbnb的房源业务，情况类似。产品一部分是构建用户预订Airbnb体验时会接触到的数字界面，另一部分是影响用户实际参与体验时的现场体验。（00:06:18）  
对我来说，这种抽象层面的思考非常吸引人。我深有体会的是：影响的对象不只是数字产品，更是消费者的实地体验。这又增加了一层复杂性。但这段经历非常有趣。我在那里待了两年半多，从产品经理做起，最终晋升为高级产品负责人。对这段经历我心怀感激，因为我深刻领悟了产品与市场适配的奥秘，也学到了许多产品质量管理的真知灼见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else you took away from that experience? Because I was at Airbnb at the same time. We never really got to work together. But I just heard amazing things about you on the experiences team. And experiences was a wild ride, from what I understand. Is there anything that you took away from that experience that kind of has stuck with you as a PM?
turns.zh: 你从那段经历中还有其他收获吗？因为我当时也在Airbnb工作。虽然我们没机会共事，但我听说过你和体验团队合作的精彩故事。据我所知，体验团队的经历堪称疯狂之旅。你有没有从中获得的收获，至今仍对你作为产品经理有所启发？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. So part of it is more of just the way Airbnb works is something that I think I use every day in my job, which is just truly thinking about product quality and the end consumer experience. And Airbnb does not ship product if it is not good. And even if they're trying new things, they are obsessed with the end consumer experience. And I learned so much from that line of thinking because just, if it shipped, it was really high quality. All the edge cases had been thought through. And the experience I had before that was definitely we were shipping things more quickly, things weren't always perfect. And it's not to say that everything Airbnb ships is perfect, but I think that obsession with the end consumer experience really influences the quality of their product suite and is something I try to bring to my job today because no one does it better, in my personal opinion.
turns.zh: 是的。Airbnb的运作方式中有一些关键点，我认为这些理念在我的日常工作中也同样适用——那就是始终以产品质量和终端用户体验为核心。如果产品不达标，Airbnb绝不会将其推向市场。即便在尝试新事物时，他们也始终以用户体验为重心。我从这种思维模式中学到了很多，因为只要产品最终上线，就必定是高质量的。所有极端情况都经过了充分考量。此前我所经历的流程则完全不同——我们往往会更急于推送产品，成果却未必尽如人意。这并不是说Airbnb推出的所有产品都完美无缺，但我认为他们对终端用户体验的执着追求确实提升了产品质量。就我个人而言，我正努力将这种理念融入自己的工作中，因为在这一领域，没有任何公司能做得更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd love to unpack that a little bit. There's kind of two questions in my mind. Is there an example of that at Airbnb where it's just like, okay, here's how they keep quality so high? And then do you have any advice for just how to do that as a company?
turns.zh: 我想深入探讨一下您的观点。我的脑海中浮现两个问题：一是Airbnb在保持产品质量方面是否有具体案例？二是作为企业，您对此有何建议？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. So I don't think that's easy for sure. One of the things Airbnb did for experiences is we had this balancing metric, which was basically using the review rate as sort our end all, be all top line goal. So you can imagine a business like that. Obviously we needed to have revenue kind of moving through the platform, and we cared about high level bookings. But really at the end of the day in the beginning, we were obsessed with making sure every person who booked actually had a good experience when they showed up to experiences. (00:09:08): And so especially if you are building early product, really thinking about how can you pick some good quality metrics that might actually balance or conflate with growth metrics, and use that as sort of your north star because it really helped the whole team to understand what they were actually trying to do at the end of the day. Growth was important, sure. Obviously we needed to grow for a lot of reasons. But the most important thing was that the actual customer experience was great. And I know Airbnb does that in other places too, but that really was experience's top line goal was our review rate and quality and it trickled down for sure.
turns.zh: 是的。这确实不易。Airbnb在体验管理方面采取的做法之一，是设定一个平衡指标——将用户评价率作为首要的核心指标。可以想象，这样的商业模式显然需要确保平台收入稳定，预订量保持高位。但在初期阶段，我们真正执着于确保每位参与体验的用户都能获得良好的体验。（00:09:08）特别是在早期产品开发阶段，关键在于如何选择能够与增长指标相平衡或融合的优质指标，并将其作为核心导向。这不仅有助于整个团队理解最终目标，也让增长目标的实现变得顺理成章。增长固然重要，但出于多重考量，我们必须确保用户体验始终卓越。我知道Airbnb在其他领域也采用了类似策略，但体验管理的核心指标——用户评价率和质量标准，始终是重中之重，其影响力自然而然地渗透到整个组织的方方面面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How did they operationalize that? Because it sounds great. Cool, let's make sure everything, all the reviews are five star. How do you build that into the way the team operates and tracks their success?
turns.zh: 他们是如何具体落实的？听起来很棒。好的，那如何将这些理念融入团队运作和绩效评估体系中呢？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. So a big part of that was actually operational, which was just making sure that hosts who weren't meeting those specific rigorous standards. There was a lot of coaching and education that was happening. Some of that was in the product and some of it wasn't. It was something that was discussed at all of the meetings that we had across everyone's teams, right? Everyone understood that it was important. And so I think that really impacted both the ops team as well as the product team who are literally building the product that would bring that to life. And I think just thinking from, especially if you're a founder and you're thinking about building your sort of early metrics, there's a lot of ways to really make sure your team really understands what that means. (00:10:33): Another thing we did a lot on the experiences team is we just dogfooded all the time. And so we were lucky in that it's a really fun product to dogfood. We were taking experiences all over the world all the time. But it really helped because you would know right away when you showed up to an event, if you were going to have a five star experience or if it was not going to be great. I mean that really helped us too because then we would go back to the teams and be like, "All right, we were just in San Francisco. We were on an experience last night, and it did not go well. What do we do about it?" So there's lots of ways to do it. But dogfooding is a good one.
turns.zh: 是的。其中很重要的一部分实际上是运营层面的，就是确保那些不符合严格标准的主持人得到改进。我们进行了大量指导和培训。有些改进体现在产品设计中，有些则不然。在我们团队的所有会议上，这都是重点讨论的内容，对吧？每个人都明白这很重要。所以我认为这不仅对运营团队有影响，对产品团队也同样重要——毕竟产品团队正是负责将这些理念落地的。特别是对于初创公司创始人来说，如果你们正在构建早期指标，就有很多方法能让团队真正理解其含义。（00:10:33）：在体验团队，我们还经常进行内部试用。我们很幸运能开发这样一个有趣的产品来进行内部试用。我们不断在全球各地体验各种活动。但这确实很有帮助，因为当你参加某个活动时，就能立刻判断是否能获得五星级体验，还是体验不佳。这对我们也很有帮助，因为之后我们会回馈团队，说：“好的，我们刚去了旧金山，昨晚参加了一个体验活动，但效果不太理想。我们该怎么改进呢？” 总之，有很多方法可以做到这一点，但内部试用确实是个不错的方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know Brian is infamous for texting the team anytime anything isn't working right in the product. And I know he was very intimately involved in experiences. Is that something you've learned to do just to kind of like, "Hey team, I found a big problem. Let's fix it." Or do you try to avoid that and not create that stress?
turns.zh: 我知道布莱恩因一有产品出现问题就给团队发消息而闻名，而且他还深度参与了体验业务。你们有没有学到这种做法，即当发现问题时直接对团队说：“嘿，团队，我发现了一个大问题，咱们一起解决吧。” 还是说你们尽量避免这种方式，避免给团队带来压力？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: I mean I think sometimes that can be a healthy stress if you do it in the right way. The nice thing I think is just making autonomous teams that feel like it is their goal to bring that quality experience to life can help you avoid some of that. But I do think that pushing teams to use the product so they firsthand experience when it is not great is a really good way to give teams sort of the motivation to act on fixing things like that. But I don't know that I text people, but I'm on Slack all the time. So if anything, I'm going to Slack you.
turns.zh: 我觉得如果方法得当，这种压力其实是良性的。我认为组建自主团队，让他们觉得自己的目标是提供优质体验，这样能帮助避免一些压力。不过我确实认为推动团队使用产品，让他们亲身感受到产品不佳的情况，是激励团队改进的有效方法。不过我倒不常发消息，但我一直在用Slack。所以如果有问题，我会在Slack上联系你们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great. Okay. Maybe one more question on this topic because it's so interesting. So on experiences you measured, I imagine, percentage of trips that were five star. Are there other quality metrics that you've used at other companies that you found helpful for keeping track of product quality and maintaining product quality?
turns.zh: 好。好的。关于这个话题，可能再问一个问题，因为它太有趣了。对于体验业务，你们会衡量五星级体验的比例吧？在其他公司，你们还用过哪些有用的质量指标来追踪产品质量和维护产品质量？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. So another one that we used at Etsy, which was an interesting one, is we realized that, so one of the pieces of product that I owned was the onboarding flow. So it was onboarding new sellers specifically. And you can imagine if you're owning that flow, you're just going to be like, all right, we just need a ton of sellers, and we need them to open their shops right away. So we started and we went down that path. And then we realized we actually tanked a couple of downstream metrics that we didn't really understand at first. And those metrics were basically getting sellers to a first sale. So we opened up a lot of shops, but they actually weren't successful when they were on the platform, and they weren't successful in a certain amount of time. (00:12:37): So we did a lot of unpacking of what happened there, why did we do that, and actually does that matter? And the end answer was, yes, it matters greatly. When Etsy sellers are opening their shop, it's really important that you get them a sale right away because it's a huge motivator, right? If you make a sale in your first day, you're like, "Oh wow. Okay, this is a thing. I could make money doing this. This is exciting. I get to ship something to my buyer." If it takes you seven days, you start to be like, "Oh no. I'm not good enough. I'm terrible at this." 10 days, into 30 days, it really impacts people. (00:13:06): And so we actually put more friction in the onboarding flow to help to start to solve for that. So we actually slowed you down. We made you be more thoughtful about what you were listing. And by doing that, we actually helped you get to a first sale faster. And so that was another good example of a quality metric that we used, which was, I think it was first sale in seven days. I might be wrong. But something along those lines. And it actually conflated with the high level growth metrics, but it was a huge quality predictor, and it was really important for long term seller success.
turns.zh: 是的。在Etsy，我们还用过另一个有趣的案例。我们意识到，我负责的其中一个产品模块是新卖家入门流程。具体来说，是专门针对新卖家的入职引导。可以想象，如果你负责这个流程，可能会想，嗯，我们只需要大量新卖家开店，然后让他们尽快上线就行了。但后来我们发现，这么做实际上损害了后续的一些关键指标——比如让卖家完成首笔交易。（00:12:37）：我们深入分析了原因，思考为什么会这样，到底有没有必要这么做。最终的结论是，非常有必要。当Etsy的新卖家开店时，尽快让他们完成首笔交易至关重要，因为这能极大激发他们的积极性。如果首日就能成交，他们会觉得“哇，太棒了。这事儿能赚钱，太兴奋了。我要给买家发货啦。”但如果要等七天、甚至30天，他们就会开始怀疑自己：“哦，不行，我不行，我做得太烂了。” （00:13:06）：所以我们在入职流程中增加了更多阻力，让卖家更谨慎地选择上架商品。通过这种方式，他们反而能更快完成首笔交易。这是我们使用的一个优质指标的典型案例，我记得当时的目标是七天内完成首笔交易，可能记错了，但差不多是这个意思。它与宏观增长指标高度关联，却是长期卖家成功的关键预测指标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So interesting. That's such a good topic. And I feel like we could explore that for an hour, but maybe for a little bit longer. Was that metric the metric that you used to measure supply growth at that point? Or was it alongside just general growth?
turns.zh: 太有意思了。这真是个很棒的话题。我觉得我们可以再聊一个小时，不过可能时间更长一点。那个指标是当时用来衡量供应增长的吗？还是和整体增长一起衡量的？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah, it was alongside general growth. It wasn't our top, top OKR. But it mattered because, again, it's sort of like you think about these things a bit as a seesaw, right? We basically were balancing our growth with making sure people were successful. And the more equilibrium you had there, the better it was for their overarching marketplace. And it's similar if you think about experiences too, right? Where, all right, you could just be growing, but people are having a terrible experience. So how do you balance those two things? And if you can get those two things in balance, you're going to cruise, and you're going to be more successful longer term.
turns.zh: 是的，和整体增长一起衡量的。但它不是我们的首要OKR。不过很重要，因为这就像跷跷板效应，对吧？我们本质上是在平衡增长和确保用户成功。平衡得越好，整个市场就越健康。体验方面也是如此，对吧？如果只是一味追求增长，但用户体验很差，那怎么平衡这两者呢？如果能在这两者之间找到平衡点，就能顺风顺水，更长远地取得成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. At Airbnb when I was working on supply growth, our main goal for the supply growth team was similar. And that was actually the goal we had, which is new listings that got their first booking. We only counted listings that had one booking as new supply. Everything else didn't really count. Because we knew that if it got booked at least once, at least it's got some level of quality and people want that place, and it's valuable to the marketplace. Okay. So you were at Airbnb, and where'd you go next?
turns.zh: 明白了。我在Airbnb负责供应增长时，我们供应增长团队的主要目标也类似。我们当时的目标是新房源获得首笔预订。我们只把有首笔预订的房源算作新供应，其他房源都不算。因为我们知道，如果一个房源至少获得一次预订，就说明它有一定质量，人们认可它，对市场有价值。好的。那你在Airbnb之后，又去哪儿了？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. So I went to a startup. And for lack of a better way to describe this, they were basically kind of building a marketplace as well, but it was more of a marketplace of ideas. And I hate when people say that, because I think it's cheesy, but it's true. They had physical co-working spaces, and they were trying to take some of the magic that was happening in their spaces. So people meeting each other, networking, people getting funding for their startups, et cetera. And they wanted to bring it online and they wanted to try to scale it so it wasn't constrained inside of their four walls. So I helped them basically come up with a longer term strategy, start to figure out how to unpack that, and get product market fit. And then also just build a technology team around trying to solve that. (00:15:16): And so that started late 2019. And then I was out for a bit, had a baby. And came back and then COVID happened. And they were a physical co-working business. That was where their majority revenue came from. And so COVID was pretty horrible for what they were trying to do. They also had some other cultural issues, and so the whole thing kind of paused/fell over. So I actually spent a year hiring a team and then had to lay them off, which was a great lesson in leadership. I'm not going to lie. I learned a lot about how to lead in that experience. (00:15:49): But after that, and it was COVID, I had a eight month old, and so I spent time actually just vibing with my kids, which was kind of fun. And then ended up going to Shopify after that. And so I was looking for a more bigger scaled, not startup, and was trying to find something a little bit more something where I could be longer term and was more excited about, and took a platform role at Shopify. And so that was really interesting in that I had, honestly, for the most part spent the majority of my career in super consumer facing roles. And the role that I took was more platform. (00:16:20): And I realized that, honestly, pretty quickly after I took the role, I was like, oh, good to know. I didn't really understand what this job was and now I know what it is, but it does not give me energy. And so I felt like I had a lot of red energy every day. And so I made a call pretty quickly to bounce, which was actually another good learning experience. I think I've gotten a lot. As I've advanced through my career, have learned a lot about what gives me Nickey Skarstad energy and have been really prioritizing that, especially in a post-COVID world. (00:16:46): And so left Shopify, and made my way to Duolingo. And so Duolingo has been super fun. I've been there since September of 2021. And in the process of helping them kind of think through a zero to one product challenge, something that's newer. Can't really talk about it unfortunately, but has been another sort of product market fit thinking exercise. It reminds me a little bit of some of the work that I did on experiences. And so it's been actually pretty challenging. It's super fun. So I'm also having a great time here as well.
turns.zh: 是啊。所以我去了一家初创公司。说实话，他们也算是在搭建一个市场平台，但更像是一个创意市场。我特别讨厌别人用这种说法，因为觉得太俗气了，但事实确实如此。他们有实体共享办公空间，试图将空间内发生的魔力搬到线上。比如人们在这里社交、建立人脉、为初创公司融资等等。他们想把这些体验数字化，并扩大规模，不再局限于四面墙之内。所以我主要帮他们制定长期战略，拆解问题，实现产品与市场的适配。然后还组建了一个技术团队来解决这些难题。（00:15:16）这项工作始于2019年底。之后我离开了一段时间，生了孩子。回来后正逢新冠疫情，他们的实体共享办公业务是主要收入来源，疫情对他们的业务打击很大。再加上内部文化问题，整个项目停摆了。结果我花了一年时间组建团队，最后又不得不裁员，这真是管理方面的深刻教训。说实话，我从中收获了很多领导经验。（00:15:49）但疫情过后，我带着八个月大的孩子，专心陪伴他们，倒也挺有趣的。之后我去了Shopify，寻找更大规模的公司，放弃初创公司，转而寻求能长期投入且更令我兴奋的职位，最终担任了Shopify的平台类角色。这份工作让我深有感触，因为我职业生涯的大部分时间都专注于面向消费者的角色，而这次的平台角色让我意识到，坦白说，我很快就发现这份工作不符合我的热情。每天都充满负能量。于是我很快决定离开，这又是一次宝贵的成长经历。随着职业生涯的发展，我逐渐明白什么能激发我的热情，并在后疫情时代将其置于优先地位。（00:16:20）离开Shopify后，我加入了Duolingo。这里超级有趣。我从2021年9月开始工作。在帮助他们思考零到一的产品挑战的过程中，尽管项目尚未公开，但这又是一次产品与市场适配的探索。它让我想起之前在体验设计方面的工作，挑战性十足，但乐趣无穷。我在这里也过得很开心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. The companies you worked at is incredible and there's so much I want to explore there. Going back to Shopify briefly, a lot of PMs, I imagine, are trying to decide should they stay where they're at? Should they go explore other places? So you said the thing that kind of pulled you out there was just the platform role didn't feel like a fit for you. Do you have any advice for folks on just how to know if a role or a company isn't a fit for them?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你曾就职的那些公司真是令人惊叹，我也特别想去探索一番。再简单聊聊Shopify吧，我想很多产品经理都在纠结：是继续留在现有岗位，还是去探索其他机会？你提到促使你离开的主要原因是平台型角色不适合你。对于那些不确定某个职位或公司是否适合自己的人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. So I think I really learned that while I was there, and also I want to make sure I actually had a great experience at Shopify and I think it is an awesome company. I would highly recommend people work there, especially if they like platform product work. One of the things I did when I was like, I don't know if I love this is I actually went through my calendar and I changed the colors of all of the meetings on my calendar to red, yellow, and green after I had the meeting. And I looked. And basically if it was yellow, I was like, okay. It was a fine meeting. My energy was baseline. If it was red, I was either bored or I was stressed, or I was not having a good time. And if it was green, it gave me energy and I felt excited and I wanted to keep working on that. (00:18:17): And when I looked back at the last few weeks, it was almost all red and yellow. And I was like, okay, this is really from an energy standpoint, I don't think I love this. And so I would say think about the work that you're doing and that lens. Get really good at figuring out what are the things that you love most about being a product person, and how can you optimize your next role for those things that you love? (00:18:39): We should talk a little bit more about this, but each company has a very different product org. And the day to day of your job as a product manager, depending on where you go in the product that you're building, is very different. And so really thinking through what that work looks like, what their process is, who your end consumer is, what will the actual work you be doing every day, what will that be? And if you can get really clear on that, and then get clear on what gives you energy and what you love, it makes it a lot easier to figure out where you should go next.
turns.zh: 是的。我在那里工作期间确实深有体会。我也想确保自己在Shopify度过了愉快的时光，我认为这是一家很棒的公司。我强烈推荐大家去那里工作，尤其是对平台产品工作感兴趣的人。我当时的做法是，当我觉得自己不喜欢某个职位时，我会回顾自己的日程安排，在开完会后，把日历上的所有会议标记成红色、黄色和绿色。然后我会分析，如果是黄色的，说明这是一次普通会议，我的精力处于正常水平；如果是红色的，说明我要么感到无聊，要么感到压力重重，要么玩得不开心；如果是绿色的，说明这让我充满活力，兴奋不已，迫切想继续投入工作。（00:18:17）回顾过去几周的日程，几乎全是红色和黄色的。我意识到，从精力层面来看，我确实不喜欢这份工作。所以我的建议是，仔细思考自己正在做的工作，从这个角度出发。深入挖掘自己最热爱产品经理工作的哪些方面，然后优化下一个职位，使其与这些热爱之处相契合。（00:18:39）我们应该再深入探讨一下，但每个公司的产品组织架构都大不相同。产品经理的日常工作，取决于你在产品中所处的位置，差别巨大。因此，真正理解这份工作的具体内容、他们的工作流程、你的终端用户是谁、你每天实际要做的工作内容，这些都至关重要。如果你能把这些想清楚，再明确什么能给你能量、什么是你热爱的，那就能更轻松地找到下一步该去哪里了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I love that tactic. I've never heard of that. Just going back to the meetings that you have in measuring, just reflecting on how much energy that meeting gave you. Great tip. Thank you for sharing that. And I'll also double down on Shopify is an amazing place to work. Just to make that clear. It's probably one of the few places I recommend PMs go try to work at.
turns.zh: 哇。我喜欢这个策略。我从未听说过这种方法。回到你提到的会议评估，就是反思会议给你带来的能量。这真是个好建议。谢谢你分享这些。另外，我还要强调Shopify确实是个很棒的工作场所。以免有误解，这可能是我唯一推荐产品经理去尝试工作的公司之一。

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. I think especially if you're newer in your PM career, they just have a really great organization. And I think it's a great place to learn how to PM. Also their product, it's a huge scaled product. And so it's complicated to build in. So I think it's a great place to really understand second order systems and systems thinking. And especially if that type of work gives you energy, I would recommend that people look for jobs there. But again, get really good at what you love. And I think what I've realized longer term is I really like the zero to one early stage. How do we get product market fit? And how do we really think through the early experience? And Shopify is at a very different stage than that. They're doing that in a couple places for sure, but that's not their day to day. And so that was interesting.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得，尤其是如果你在产品经理的职业生涯中还算新手的话，他们的组织架构真的很棒。我认为这里是学习产品管理的绝佳之地。此外，他们的产品规模庞大，开发起来颇具挑战。因此，这里能让你深刻理解二阶系统和系统思维。特别是如果这类工作能激发你的热情，我会建议大家去那里求职。但说真的，要在自己热爱的事情上做到精通。我发现从长远来看，我特别喜欢从零到一的早期阶段——如何实现产品与市场的匹配，以及如何深思熟虑地设计初期体验。但Shopify正处于一个完全不同的阶段。他们在某些领域确实在做这类工作，但这并非他们的日常业务。所以这点挺有趣的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. That makes a lot of sense. Going back to what you just touched on, the idea of product org and structure and how different companies build product, there's kind of two ways to approach this and take whichever direction you want. Which of the companies you've worked at did you enjoy most, and that's kind of stuck with you as a way you want to build product? Or just like, how would you approach building a product org in cross-functional teams versus not, and reporting lines, things like that? What do you recommend there?
turns.zh: 嗯，这说得很有道理。回到你刚刚提到的产品组织和架构，以及不同公司如何构建产品的问题，这里有两种不同的思路和方向。那么你在任职过的公司中，哪家最令你难忘，并且对你的产品构建理念影响深远？或者说，你如何看待在跨职能团队中构建产品组织与不构建产品组织的区别，以及汇报层级之类的？对此你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. So I feel like you're asking me to pick a favorite child, which especially as a mother, that's hard to do. But no, I don't know. I feel like I've learned things from a lot of these different places and it's hard to choose. I think some of my early work at Etsy was very formative, and it was where I learned how to be a product manager. And so I feel very proud of that. I also think Etsy was out there building in public. I'm literally doing air quotes right now. I know you can't see me.
turns.zh: 是啊。这感觉就像让我选一个最爱的孩子，作为一个母亲，这确实很难。但说真的，我觉得很难抉择。我在Etsy的早期工作对我影响深远，在那里我学会了如何成为一名产品经理。对此我深感自豪。我还觉得Etsy当时在公开开发方面做得很出色。我现在用引号的手势表示强调，虽然你们看不到我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can see them.
turns.zh: 我能看到。

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: But they were doing that because they had such a passionate, involved, engaged early community that they could not just ship things and have them land well if they did not involve their community early. So they were doing prototyping, beta testing, and basically getting people to try things and give feedback on things. I honestly, I think before a lot of people were, and that was something at the time that was really interesting and has really stayed with me, it's how to work with community and how to build community around the product that you're building. (00:21:25): Because at the end of the day, especially when it's early days, it really helps scale, get people to evangelize what you're building, help teach other people how to use it, things like that. And so I learned how to do that at Etsy. And I think that was super formative. And then also just Airbnb, what we talked about before, and just deeply baking in product quality and the end consumer experience into everything that you're building is also something I literally apply every day. So if I had to choose, it would be those two places, but I plan on continuing to learn.
turns.zh: 但他们之所以能做到这样，是因为他们早期就拥有一个充满热情、积极参与、深度投入的社区。如果不让社区早期参与其中，他们就无法顺利发布产品并获得良好的反馈。因此，他们会进行原型设计、Beta测试，让人们尝试产品并提供反馈。说实话，我认为当时很多人都没有意识到这一点，而这在当时确实很有趣，也一直让我铭记于心——如何与社区合作，如何围绕正在开发的产品建立社区。（00:21:25）因为归根结底，尤其是在早期阶段，这确实有助于扩大规模，让人们为你开发的产品宣传造势，帮助其他人学会使用产品等等。我在Etsy学到了这些东西，我认为这对我的成长非常重要。还有Airbnb，我们之前讨论过的，将产品质量和终端用户体验深深融入到你所构建的一切产品中，这也是我每天都在践行的。所以如果非要选的话，我会选这两家公司，但我计划继续学习。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. Both very community driven businesses.
turns.zh: 有意思。这两家公司都非常注重社区驱动。

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: True.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then in terms of how they structured their org, is there anything there about just here's what I've learned works best for how to build product teams, structure product teams, that stuck with you?
turns.zh: 接下来是关于他们如何构建产品团队的组织架构。是否有任何经验总结，能告诉我们如何最有效地组建产品团队、构建产品团队架构，并且让这些经验至今仍令你印象深刻？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. So I think there's kind of two overarching popular organizational modes for product org specifically. There's either the functional organization where everyone in the product team will report up through either a VP product, or a chief product officer, or something along those lines. And I think that actually really works in certain circumstances and is great. And typically how that works is you'll have your product partners, your trifecta, if you will, you have your design partner and your engineering partner, they will typically also report up into functional leadership. I think in bigger organizations that really works well, especially when you have orgs that need a lot of development in the function. So you'll have a lot of either APMs or product managers who are newer in their career and need a lot of support in development. And I think those functional ways of building makes sense. When I was at Etsy, that was the way that the reporting structure was and it made a lot of sense. (00:23:00): And then on the flip side, actually, when I was at Airbnb, because experiences was this new pretty nascent business opportunity, it had a GM structure. And so basically the whole product org that worked on experiences laddered up into a business leader and that business leader managed all of the functions. So they were the manager of the operations team, the marketing folks, product, and whatever. And I actually think that really worked for team like experiences at a company like Airbnb because what it did is it gave the leader of that business a ton of autonomy to really figure out what does this business need to be successful? And they didn't have to rely on, I guess they did in some ways, but not 100% rely on the larger company's resources to get the work that they needed done. (00:23:44): And I actually think that had they launched experiences inside of the Etsy style of organizational structure, it never would've succeeded because it had such a unique business need, and it needed its own process and ways of building product, et cetera. And because they sort of, hate to say wall it off, because it wasn't fully walled off, but because they gave it its own space and its own structure, it allowed it to succeed because they were able to fund it in the right way, give it the resources that it needed, et cetera. (00:24:14): So I've seen those two types of models work. And I think if I was a founder and I was building my initial product org, how I would think about it was basically what are we trying to build? What is the product? And then what type of process do we need to put in place for us to figure out how do we build it? And then what type of people do we need? And then really taking a step back to really figure out, all right, organizationally, how do we shape this so we can make sure that those people have autonomy and they have what they need to just be able to cruise? So I honestly don't think there's a right way. I know that's a non-answer. I think it really depends on what you're trying to build and the stage at which you're at.

是的。我认为针对产品团队，常见的两种主流组织模式是：一是职能型组织，即产品团队的所有成员都向产品副总裁、首席产品官或类似职位汇报。我认为这种模式在某些情况下确实非常有效，比如当组织需要在某个职能领域大力发展时，比如有很多初级产品经理或产品经理需要大量支持时，职能型架构就能很好地发挥作用。我在Etsy工作时就是这种汇报结构，效果非常好。
（00:23:00）另一方面，Airbnb的情况则相反。当时体验业务部门是一个新兴且尚未成熟的机遇领域，因此采用了总经理制。整个产品团队围绕体验业务汇报给业务负责人，由他统管所有职能部门——运营团队、市场团队、产品团队等。这种模式非常适合Airbnb这样的公司，因为它赋予了业务负责人极大的自主权，让他们能够自主判断业务成功所需的条件，而不必完全依赖公司资源来完成工作。
（00:23:44）我认为，如果Airbnb的体验团队采用Etsy式的组织结构，它永远不会成功，因为该业务有着独特的需求，需要专属的流程和产品构建方式。Airbnb之所以成功，是因为他们为其划定了独立的空间和架构，使其能够灵活调配资源，顺利推进项目。
（00:24:14）我见证过这两种模式的成效。若我作为创始人组建初期产品团队，我会首先思考：我们要打造什么？产品是什么？为此需要怎样的流程？又需要怎样的团队？然后退后一步审视组织架构，确保团队拥有自主权和所需资源，从而顺畅推进项目。说实话，没有标准答案。这取决于你要构建的产品类型和所处的阶段。

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I think especially if your business is new, going functional makes sense because you don't necessarily have a lot of organizational complexity. Airbnb at the time we were there, Lenny, was a huge company, right? It had tons of different teams that were trying to tackle many different problems. So that GM model made a lot of sense because it again was able to take a specific business opportunity, give it the resources that it need, and give it space to run. When your company's smaller stage, I think that matters less. Typically, especially if you're working on solving similar problems as an organization, functional makes a ton of sense. Because then you're also thinking more holistically about, all right, how do we build the right product development process across different functions to make sure that we are, to use a bad metaphor, it's like the symphony metaphor. You have all these different instruments that need to figure out how do we play together at the right times? And I think that functional way of working actually allows you to do that really well.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，特别是如果你的公司是新创企业，采用职能型组织结构是比较合理的，因为你不一定面临太多的组织复杂性。比如我们去Airbnb的时候，那个时候的Airbnb已经是一家大型公司了，对吧？它有许多不同的团队，试图解决各种各样的问题。因此，通用管理模式（GM model）就显得非常实用，因为它能够抓住特定的商业机会，为其提供所需资源，并给予其自主运作的空间。当你的公司规模较小时，我认为这点就没那么重要了。通常来说，尤其是当你的组织正在解决相似问题时，职能型组织结构会非常有效。因为这样你就能更全面地思考：好吧，我们如何在不同职能部门之间建立正确的产品开发流程，确保我们——用一个不恰当的比喻来说——就像管弦乐队的比喻。所有不同的乐器都需要协调好何时一起演奏？而我认为这种职能型的工作方式实际上能让你很好地做到这一点。

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. Well one, I want to know who you talked to. That's terrifying. Hopefully they said good things. You don't have to out them.

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yes. Well I'm glad to hear that because that actually is some of the work that I honestly love the most. And when I look at my calendar, those are moments where I am green energy. And so I have some first principles that I like to apply when I'm thinking about setting high level vision and strategy. And the first is make sure that you pull in your people and your team. I've seen a lot of director level people through my career who will try to work on strategy in a vacuum alone. They'll write a document and they'll be like, "Okay, team. Here's what we're doing. Here's our strategy." And it never goes well. And it doesn't go well. It might be the right strategy, but because you did not bring people along on that journey to come up with it, they did not feel like they had a hand in crafting it themselves. They are often not bought in, and getting people to buy in when they haven't been involved is very challenging and time consuming. We don't got time, right? (00:28:40): And so I think that's my first principle is just bring along the team. And I think there are ways to do that where you're not voting on strategy. You should not be voting. I think good product work is often not democratic, right? You need a clear leader who understands a lot of the signals and understands the larger competitive marketplace that can make decisions. And I think, especially when you're thinking about strategy, it's great to get input, but ultimately at the end of the day, you should have one person who is responsible for it. (00:29:06): And the other thing is a lot of times people don't really talk to leadership or the larger business leaders to get organizational context that helps them come up with the right strategy. They'll sort of build something in a vacuum, and then they'll come up with it and they'll get a ton of feedback from people across the org that were like, "Oh, this conflates with our strategy. We're doing this, and it's very similar." Or, "Our structural platform actually does not have the capability for us to do that thing." Whatever. And so just make sure that you're talking to people. And also all the way up to the CEO, and making sure the founder and the CEO is very bought in because ultimately, at the end of the day, they're choosing to resource what you're working on and are going to help you meet what you need. So those are some of the foundations for good vision and strategy work. (00:29:51): And then kind of zooming down into the weeds, I really like the vision mission strategy pyramid. I think might be a little tired. I like to think it's wired. But yeah. So if you just think about a pyramid shape, at the top is vision. Below it is mission and strategy, and then objectives. And this is a very simple framework. You honestly just Google vision mission strategy objectives, and you'll see it in Google image results. And all it is really is thinking about hitting those specific notes and thinking about them top down. So where do you need to go long term? What is the long term vision of what you're trying to do? In 10 years, if you could zoom up and look at what an ideal path for you would be, what is that? Write it down. (00:30:32): And then you start, as you go down the pyramid, you get clearer and basically you bring things down to your moment in time more clearly. So if you're thinking about your mission, all right, it's another level of abstraction of how do we make our vision come to life. And then you get into strategy. All right, how do we actually pick apart what we think is going to need to happen for us to actually be able to execute on that vision? And then your objectives can be OKRs, or whatever sort of goal setting model that you use to really one level get clear on, all right, in the next three to six months, what are the actual notes that we need to hit to be able to sing that beautiful symphony, is a terrible metaphor. 是的。很高兴听到你这么说。因为这恰恰是我最热爱的工作内容之一。当我看日历时，那些时刻就是我全身心投入绿色能源工作的时刻。关于制定高层愿景和战略，我有一些基本原则。首先，要确保团队成员的参与。我在职业生涯中见过很多总监级别的人试图独自制定战略。他们写好文件后就对团队说：“好的，大家看，我们要这么做。这是我们的战略。” 但结果往往不尽如人意。即使战略本身是正确的，但由于没有让团队成员共同参与制定，他们会觉得自己没有参与其中，自然也就缺乏认同感。让团队参与进来绝非易事，而且耗时费力——毕竟我们时间有限，对吧？  

（00:28:40）所以我认为首要原则就是要带上团队。虽然不必通过投票表决战略，但也不应搞民主决策。优秀的产品工作往往不民主——你需要一个深谙市场动态、能做出决策的清晰领导者。在制定战略时，征求意见固然重要，但最终必须由一人负责。  

（00:29:06）还有一点，很多人不善于与高层或更广泛的业务领导者沟通，获取有助于制定正确战略的组织背景信息。他们往往闭门造车，最终得到反馈时才发现与现有战略冲突，或者发现平台架构无法支持某些功能。这就是为什么要确保与各级领导沟通，包括CEO，确保创始人和CEO深度认同，因为最终是他们决定是否为你的工作提供资源支持。  

（00:29:51）接下来具体讲讲战略框架。我喜欢“愿景-使命-战略-目标”金字塔模型，虽然可能有些老生常谈，但确实有效。金字塔顶层是愿景，底层是使命和战略，再往下是具体目标。这是一个简单的框架。直接在谷歌图片上搜索“愿景-使命-战略-目标”就能找到相关图示。关键在于逐层深化思考：你要去向何方？十年后理想路径是什么？将这些写下来。  

（00:30:32）沿着金字塔逐层深入，思路会越来越清晰。比如制定使命时，要思考如何将愿景落地。再到战略层面，拆解关键步骤，确保每一步都清晰易懂。
怎样才能实现这一愿景呢？然后，你的目标可以是OKR，或者你采用的任何目标设定模式。通过这种方式，你就能清晰地了解，在接下来的三到六个月里，我们需要达成哪些实际目标，才能奏响那首美妙的交响乐。这真是个糟糕的比喻。现在我不介意承认这一点。但管他呢。

turns.en: I get it. I get it.
turns.zh: 我懂了。我懂了。

turns.en: That's evocative. While we're on that topic, actually just to interrupt briefly, how are you very practically doing this for say vision and mission? Are you starting a Google doc and writing it out, are you using Miro or FigJam, or something like that?
turns.zh: 这真引人深思。既然说到这个话题，容我插句话，你们是如何具体落实愿景和使命的？是创建一个Google文档来撰写，还是使用Miro或FigJam之类的工具？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah, so I think visioning exercise is a great moment to pull in your larger team. Because I'm remote now, I would use Miro or FigJam. Duolingo, we use FigJam typically because we are super embedded in Figma. In the past I've used MURAL. I actually personally like MURAL's whiteboarding product better. So I would open that up and I would walk through a number of things with the team and do a brainstorm literally. All right. Where do you all see us going in 10 years? What do we think what is the larger competitive landscape going to do in the next 10 years that could need to influence the work that we're doing? What are their ideas, and get everyone thinking. (00:32:05): Good brainstorm are often cross-functional. So go outside of your own team. Can you pull in somebody from marketing? Can somebody from the larger policy team sit in? How do you make it really cross-functional and really zoom up and give everyone the space and the freedom to think existential and to frame it that way,?we are going to be thinking in a five to 10 year timeline. Do not worry about what's happening today. And honestly, if you do that right, those are super fun exercises.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为愿景规划活动是召集整个团队参与的绝佳时机。由于我现在远程办公，我们通常会用Miro或FigJam。就Duolingo而言，由于我们深度依赖Figma，所以通常选择FigJam。过去我也用过MURAL。说实话，我个人更喜欢MURAL的白板功能。所以我会打开软件，和团队一起梳理各种问题，进行头脑风暴。好的。大家认为我们十年后会发展成什么样？未来十年内竞争格局会有哪些变化，可能对我们的工作产生影响？大家有什么想法，让每个人都开动脑筋。（00:32:05）：有效的头脑风暴通常需要跨职能参与。所以不妨邀请市场部的人加入，让政策团队的人也参与进来。如何让整个过程真正跨职能、真正放眼长远，给每个人空间和自由去进行深度思考？我们要从五到十年的时间维度去思考。别纠结于眼下的情况。说实话，如果组织得当，这样的活动非常有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you're doing this remotely, I imagine.
turns.zh: 嗯，我猜你是在远程进行这些工作吧。

turns.en: Yep.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so do you just kind of schedule a meeting, kick it off, point everyone to this Miro doc, for example, with a bunch of prompts and sticky notes and things like that? How do you actually practically do that?
turns.zh: 那你通常是怎么做的呢？比如说，是不是先安排个会议，启动之后，再把大家引导到Miro文档里，里面有各种提示、便利贴之类的东西？具体操作步骤是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: So I would pre-fill out the Miro beforehand. So figure out what are the things you want to discuss with your team, create them as headers in the Miro document. So when everyone lands in there, you have a very clear here's what we're talking about today. You can put that into the agenda on your calendar invite. I've actually been to some really good strategic brainstorms that will attach some kind of competitive thinking landscape in advance. So people could have a little bit of a pre-read. (00:33:06): And then when you get into the actual session, you already have the time allotments scheduled and thought through. And both Miro and FigJam have really awesome timer, and it'll play music while everyone is working. It's pretty cute. FigJam's sounds are really well done. Whoever their sound architect is, bravo. And it'll ding after, give them 10 minutes and it'll give you a nice chime, and then you can review them together and you can go through each touchpoint that you want to talk about. (00:33:33): After it's done, I like to do some synthesis together in the meeting. So basically grab ideas that are similar, bucket things into concepts that are alike. And then I will take it later and spend more time thinking about it. I think a lot of people think you have to actually come away with a vision together in a meeting that's very clear, and you don't. You can just come up with ideas, take a stab at drafting it, and get some more feedback before it's final.
turns.zh: 我会提前在Miro里把内容准备好。先想好要和团队讨论的内容，然后在Miro文档里创建标题。当大家加入会议时，就能清楚了解今天要讨论的内容。这些内容也可以添加到日历邀请的议程里。我参加过一些很棒的战略头脑风暴会，他们会提前上传竞争格局分析图，让大家有时间提前阅读相关资料。（00:33:06）然后进入实际会议时，时间分配和思路都已经规划好了。Miro和FigJam都有很棒的计时功能，工作时还会播放音乐，特别贴心。FigJam的音效设计得很棒，不知道他们的音效设计师是谁，真厉害。时间到了之后，系统会提醒大家，还有10分钟的时间，然后会有提示音，这样大家就能一起回顾每个需要讨论的关键点。（00:33:33）结束后，我通常会在会议上做一些总结，把相似的想法归类到相同的概念里。然后我会再花时间深入思考。我觉得很多人认为在会议上必须当场得出一个清晰的愿景，但其实不必如此。你可以先提出想法，尝试起草，然后在最终定稿前收集更多反馈。

turns.en: One last question on this thread, which also could be an entire hour of discussion, are there any examples of prompts or things you ideated that you could share?
