turns.zh: 关于这个话题的最后一个问题——这个问题甚至可以展开整整一个小时的讨论——你们是否有一些灵感迸发的提示或创意案例可以分享？我知道你们不能谈论在Duolingo的工作内容，但为了让大家更直观理解，你们能否举几个头脑风暴出的例子？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, so to take it back to experiences, because we've talked about that a lot, so people have some baseline context. Some of the early experiences visioning was really interesting because it was all about what type of experience can we create. And really thinking through when you've traveled in the past, what has brought you joy? Or what were the moments in your travel journey that have been really interesting, provocative, basically you remember the most, and why? And thinking through some of those things as a group. And those are good group exercises, because you're like, wow, I got to know a lot about Lenny by that crazy travel experience that he had. And so really kind of thinking through about how you craft really meaningful prompts that, again, connect to your strategy. So how does that ladder up into strategy? Obviously thinking through the experience that you're creating is going to help you come up with the right vision and fill out your pyramid in the right way, right?
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，回到经验层面，因为我们已经多次探讨过这个话题，所以大家对此已经有了一定的基础认知。早期的一些体验构想阶段非常有趣，当时我们都在思考：我们能创造怎样的体验？当你回顾过往的旅行经历时，哪些时刻曾带给你快乐？哪些旅程中的瞬间最引人入胜、最发人深省，并且最令你难忘？与团队一起探讨这些问题效果显著。比如，大家会惊叹于Lenny的疯狂旅行经历，从而对他有了更深入的了解。通过这样的方式，思考如何设计出真正有意义的提示，同时与你的战略紧密结合。那么，如何将这些构想上升到战略层面呢？显然，深入思考你正在打造的体验，将有助于你制定正确的愿景，并以正确的方式填充你的战略金字塔，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So we went on kind of on a tangent around brainstorming. Did you want to share more around just going from vision to goals to execution?
turns.zh: 好的。我们稍微偏离了主题，聊了一下头脑风暴环节。你们是否想分享更多关于从愿景到目标再到执行的具体内容？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. So I think just generally, as you walk down that strategy pyramid, really getting down into the OKRs. And I think it's important because sometimes strategy is too abstract and too high level. And it's hard for people to take the step on how do I walk up that pyramid? And that to me is where having good strategy and having good OKRs help your team do that. And so good OKRs to me are just clear articulations of your strategy, whatever it is that are important to you, and it boils it down into the next three months, here's what we're working on. And I think that is just really good for teams because, again, if you're always in the clouds, it starts to get hard to really bring things down to the feature level of we're going to create a Jira ticket for this specific thing that we need to build. It needs to connect up to a strategy and back down.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为总的来说，当你沿着战略金字塔层层推进时，深入到OKR层面至关重要。这很重要，因为有时候战略过于抽象、太高大上。人们很难理解如何沿着这个金字塔向上攀登。对此，我认为拥有良好的战略和OKR能帮助团队实现这一目标。对我来说，优秀的OKR就是对战略的清晰阐释——无论对你而言什么是重要的，都要将其浓缩到未来三个月的行动计划中。对于团队来说，这真的很有帮助，因为如果你总是高高在上，很难真正把事情落实到具体的功能层面，比如为我们需要构建的特定功能创建Jira工单。OKR需要与战略相连接，并反向推动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Where do you put, say, these OKRs? Do you just brainstorm, come up with vision and rough strategy, that translates into goals? Where do you do this? And then also just how long do you usually spend on this overall process?
turns.zh: 明白了。那么，比如说，这些OKR放在哪里呢？是先头脑风暴，提出愿景和粗略的战略，再转化为目标吗？你们在哪里进行这些工作？另外，整个过程通常会花费多长时间？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. So the way that we do it at Duolingo now is we work on quarterly OKRs. And so that process will kick off usually the third month in the quarter. Really thinking through, all right, how are we trending on our OKRs this quarter? Did we commit to the right number of things? How are we doing? And then it is going, all right, so what do we need to do next quarter? And ideally, again, that's going to plug into a longer term plan. Otherwise it feels a little messy, and it feels not grounded in a long term plan or strategy in any way, shape, or form. (00:36:36): And then, so what we'll do is spend a few weeks as a team coming up with, all right, what could the next quarter look like? What is going to add the most impact and help us execute on that long term strategy? And then how do we make sure that we're setting the right objectives and KRs below them? And then usually there's some sort of leadership review. I actually forget, Lenny, how did goal setting go at Airbnb? I honestly don't remember. It sounds terrible, but it was a while ago. I can't even remember if Airbnb used OKRs.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我们现在在Duolingo的做法是，每季度制定OKR。通常，这个过程会在季度第三个月启动。我们会仔细思考：本季度我们的OKR进展如何？我们是否设定了合适的目标数量？我们的执行情况如何？然后就是下一个季度要做什么？理想情况下，这一切都应该与长期规划相衔接。否则就会显得杂乱无章，完全缺乏长期战略的根基。（00:36:36）接下来团队会花几周时间构思：下个季度会是什么样子？哪些举措能产生最大影响，助力我们执行长期战略？然后确保设定正确的目标和支持目标的关键结果（KR）。通常还会进行领导层审查。我忘了，Lenny，Airbnb的目标设定流程是怎样的？说实话我记不清了，毕竟已经过去很久了。我甚至不确定Airbnb是否使用过OKR。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There was a long period where OKRs were a very big deal. Our head of product was really gungho on OKRs. And I think for a couple years, we were very strict OKR culture. And then it kind of evolved into just rough-
turns.zh: 曾经有一段时间，OKR备受重视。我们的产品负责人对OKR非常热衷。有一两年时间，我们严格遵循OKR文化。但后来它逐渐演变为——

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Goals.
turns.zh: 粗略的

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... interpretation of OKRs. Yeah, goals and strategy and mission and vision. And so it's kind of this morphed version at this point, as far as I know.
turns.zh: ……对OKR的解读。是的，目标、战略、使命和愿景。就我所知，现在OKR已经演变成了一个混合版本。

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Gotcha. Yeah. And I will say OKR frameworks might not be the best for every single team, but having some sort of goal framework that is shared across functions is useful no matter the size or the scale of your business. I think a lot of times people get hung up and they want to nitpick OKRs specifically. And I think some of those criticisms are very fair. But you should have some sort of framework that's shared from a process standpoint across your team that everyone can use and work on together. Because again, it takes your strategy and it brings it down into the now. So you can act on, in the next three months, you can bring something to life, and you're very clear on what that looks like.
turns.zh: 明白了。是的。我要说的是，OKR框架未必适合每个团队，但建立一个跨职能共享的目标框架总是有用的，无论你的业务规模大小如何。我觉得很多时候人们纠结于具体的OKR细节。有些批评确实有道理。但你应该为团队建立一个共享的流程框架，让大家共同使用、共同推进。因为OKR能将战略落到实处，让你知道接下来三个月要做什么，要把什么变为现实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to pull out a thread of something you mentioned earlier of how to finally make decisions. And how in your experience the PM kind of is often sort of a final decision maker. I'd love to hear any advice you have of how to set that up on a team where it's either clear the PMs have a little bit more say and/or just bring people along to a final conclusion. Is there any advice on tips and tactics used to help with that?
turns.zh: 我想延伸一下你之前提到的如何最终做出决策的话题。以你的经验来看，产品经理通常是最终决策者。我很想听听你在团队中如何建立这种机制的建议——要么明确产品经理有更大话语权，要么引导团队达成最终共识。有什么相关的建议或策略吗？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. So I actually just read this really great book that is slightly tangential, but I thought it really applied to this type of basically getting people to align on decisions. It's by Chris Voss. He is this famous FBI negotiator. I think it's called Split the Difference: Negotiating As if Your Life Depends on It. Don't quote me on that.
turns.zh: 是的。我刚读了一本相关的书，虽然有些偏题，但我觉得它对如何让人们在决策上达成一致很有启发。作者是克里斯·沃斯，他是著名的FBI谈判专家。这本书叫《分歧谈判：谈判就像命悬一线》，但具体书名可能有误。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it's Never Split the Difference, right? And then I think he's also got a masterclass which I've watched, which is really good.
turns.zh: 我想应该是《永远不要让步》吧？我还看过他的大师课，非常棒。

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: I actually haven't watched the masterclass yet, but it's on my list after reading the book. And a lot of it, I think, especially because he's an FBI person, I thought it was going to be very much, "You're going to do this." And it's all basically his whole approach is empathy, and it's repeating things back to you, making people feel heard, making sure that you're hearing why they maybe don't like your strategy, or why they think that's a bad OKR. And I think if you can spend some time just listening to your team and really understanding why is this not resonating, you can help guide people on the right path. Or you realize you're wrong. Good PMs are humble people, right? You're not always right. Not always going to be right. So how do you know when you're right and wrong is another good podcast that you should do with somebody else cause I'm probably not very at it. Yeah.
turns.zh: 实际上我还没看过那堂大师课，但读完那本书后，我把它列入了待看清单。我觉得里面有很多内容，尤其是他作为FBI人员的背景，让人以为会是那种“你必须照做”的模式。但他的整个方法论其实是基于共情——通过重复对方的观点，让人们感受到被倾听，确保你理解为什么他们可能不喜欢你的策略，或者为什么他们认为某个OKR是不合适的。我认为，如果你能花时间倾听团队的声音，真正理解为什么某个方案无法引起共鸣，你就能引导人们走上正确的道路。或者你会意识到自己错了。优秀的产品经理必须保持谦逊，对吧？你不可能永远正确，也不总是对的。所以如何判断自己是对是错，这也是值得与他人探讨的好话题，因为我可能不太擅长这方面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Good tip. I really like that.
turns.zh: 好建议。我很喜欢这一点。

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. But I think that helps. And the other thing is I love the concept of one way versus two way door decision making, right? If your team is making a really critical long-term decision that's going to be limiting to a lot of the future things that you could want or need to do, that is a one way door decision. And you should spend time really thinking about discussing it, getting feedback and buy-in from your larger community, from your leadership team, et cetera. If it is a two-way door decision, it's not going to make a huge impact, you can change it later if you need to, let your team cruise on those things. Because it gives people autonomy. It helps you move fast. And then it just makes sure that when it does come down to decisions that are harder to change longer term, then those are the moments you should spend time and really think about and discuss and debate, et cetera.
turns.zh: 是的。但我觉得这很有帮助。还有一点，我特别喜欢单向门和双向门决策的概念，对吧？如果你的团队正在做一个非常关键的长期决策，这个决策会限制你未来可能想要或需要做的事情，那就是单向门决策。你应该花时间认真讨论，收集反馈，获得更广泛的团队、领导层等的认可。如果是双向门决策，就不会产生太大影响，如果需要的话可以后续调整，让团队继续推进这些事情。因为这赋予了人们自主权，有助于你快速行动。然后当涉及到更难改变的长期决策时，那才是你应该花时间认真思考、讨论和辩论的时刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have any examples or stories that come to mind of those sorts of decisions that you kind of help people just go for it, even though I may not necessarily agree?
turns.zh: 你能想到哪些例子或故事，说明你帮助人们即使自己不一定认同也要勇往直前？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Let's see. Yeah. So one big one that we made at Airbnb that was pretty formative in early days was we came up with basically an articulation of what we thought a good experience was, and the standards that an experience needed to meet for it to be considered a good experience for us. And that was a many month long term project. And it was so important because we ended up building the product around it, building our policies around it, building how we educated our hosts around it. We had one moment in time to figure it out and get it right until it scaled everywhere. And so that was a true one way door decision where it was really hard to change later because we literally needed it to be relatively final. (00:40:53): On Etsy, there was some big decisions that were made at certain points in time around what can be sold in the marketplace, and how to think through what constitutes something that is hand made. Those were one way door decisions, right? It's really hard to change that later because it's going to influence all of the listings that you have in your ecosystem. And so I think really thinking through those types of things are important and really setting teams up to be able to pause and spend some time to get it right because it will influence the end product in a very real way.
turns.zh: 让我想想。是的。Airbnb早期做的一个重大决定，对我们影响深远。我们基本上明确了我们认为好的体验是什么，以及一个体验需要满足哪些标准才能被我们视为好的体验。这是一个历时数月的长期项目。它非常重要，因为我们最终围绕它来构建产品，制定政策，培训房东。我们只有一次机会在它大规模推广前把它想清楚、做正确。这是一个真正的单向门决策，之后很难再更改，因为我们确实需要它相对最终确定。（00:40:53）：在Etsy上，他们在某些时候做了一些重大决定，比如市场上可以销售什么商品，以及如何界定手工艺品。这也是单向门决策，对吧？之后很难再更改，因为这会影响你生态系统中的所有商品列表。所以我认为认真思考这类问题很重要，让团队能够暂停下来，花时间把事情做对，因为这会对最终产品产生非常真实的影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you know if it's a one way or a two way door decision? Do you find that it's generally pretty obvious when you're making the decision, or is it sometimes like, oh shit, we should have thought about that more?
turns.zh: 怎样判断一个决策是单向的还是双向的？你会发现，在做决策时通常比较明显，但有时也会突然意识到：天哪，我们本该多考虑一下！

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. I would say I think I'm good at this 80% of the time these days, just because I've seen it done wrong in a lot of ways. But I think it's a muscle that you build honestly, and you get better over time about thinking about second order thinking. And so it's starting to understand, all right, if I make this decision today, it's going to impact this next level of decisions and the next level after that. And that will cascade through our larger system. (00:41:56): A great book to read if you are a product person is Thinking in Systems by Donella Meadows. It's just about really thinking through how systems work, and then you can start to extrapolate what is the second order effect of the system. And if you think about that through your own ecosystem, it starts to help you understand, all right, this is a linchpin in our larger ecosystem that we got to be really careful about if we're going to touch it or change it longer term. But I do think some of that it's muscle, you build it over time. You make a couple of mistakes sometimes, and then you have to realize the true consequences of those mistakes and you don't make it again.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得如今我能在80%的情况下处理好这种情况，因为我见过太多决策失误的例子。但说实话，这确实需要不断磨练，你会逐渐学会从更宏观的角度思考问题。比如，当你今天做出一个决定时，它会影响到下一步的决策，甚至更深层次的决策。这些影响会层层叠加，波及整个系统。（00:41:56）：如果你是一名产品经理，推荐阅读唐纳·米多斯的《系统思维》。这本书深入探讨了系统运作的机制，让你能推演出系统的“二阶效应”。将这种思维应用到自己的生态系统中，你会逐渐明白：某些关键节点是我们整个生态系统的支柱，若要长期调整或改造它们，必须谨慎行事。不过这确实需要不断练习，有时你会犯错，但必须深刻认识这些错误的后果，才能避免重蹈覆辙。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can we talk a bit more about the second order decision framework? I know you have a awesome newsletter post about this, and it was something I wanted to chat about. Is this a framework that PMs can use to make better decisions? And I guess how could they do that? And then maybe just describe a little bit more about just this concept of second order decisions, because it sounds really important.
turns.zh: 能否详细谈谈二阶决策框架？我知道你写过一篇精彩的通讯文章，正是这个话题让我很感兴趣。产品经理能否借助这个框架做出更明智的决策？具体该如何操作？能否进一步解释二阶决策的概念？听起来这很重要。

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. Basically what second order thinking is is you being able to think beyond the decisions that you're making today. The decisions you make today will affect tomorrow's decisions and your ability to build on your decisions that you made today. And this feels very existential and meta, but why it's important is that, especially when you're building product, is there's a cost associated with your time of everything you build. Especially when you're building marketplaces or anything with UGC content. When you make a change today, and it impacts every single user in your ecosystem that then is going to act on that change, it's really hard to make those changes later. (00:43:23): Let's talk about Airbnb home listing as an example. Really thinking through what are the pieces of data or all the pieces of data in the system that we need to actually list a home. And then how do we use those throughout our whole system in different ways? And then anytime you have to change those things. So that could be little simple things like truncating the length of the title of an Airbnb home when it's listed on the platform. You're going to have mad hosts, you're going to have design changes that need to be made to make sure that they can actually display something in a different way. It gets just inherently more complex the more complex your system is. So that is probably a terribly described way of describing second order thinking.
turns.zh: 没错。二阶思维本质上是指你要跳出当下决策的局限，预见未来决策的连锁反应。这些决策会影响明天的决策，甚至影响你构建当下决策的能力。这听起来有些抽象，但其重要性在于：尤其是在产品开发中，每个决策都需要耗费时间成本。以Airbnb房源列表为例，必须梳理清楚整个系统中用于列出房源的所有数据要素。每当你要调整这些数据时，都会影响到生态系统中的每个用户。若要修改这些数据，比如限制房源标题长度，就会引发房东的抱怨，需要进行设计调整以确保信息展示方式的统一。系统越复杂，挑战就越大。这或许是二阶思维最难理解的部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes total sense. And that's something we dealt with it, sorry to interrupt, but that's like on the host team, we dealt with this question often of just any change you make and the listing flow is going to impact so much of the experience of a host and a guest. And so that makes total sense. Sorry, keep going.
turns.zh: 这完全说得通。很抱歉打断一下，我们确实遇到过这种情况——在主办团队中，我们经常处理这样的问题：只要你做出任何变更，房源列表的流程就会对房东和房客的体验产生巨大影响。所以这完全说得通。抱歉，请继续。

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. No, and I think that forcing yourself and your team to think in that way is just a really good thinking exercise because it will save you time and it will save you money, a lot of money later, if you don't constantly have to rebuild things when you want to make changes to your system later. And that ladders up again into having a very clear vision and a strategy. Because what you're doing is you're starting to think on the long horizon. And so the decisions that you're making today are in service of that long horizon. So you can actually build in that direction and you don't constantly have to rebuild every time you're trying to change something.
turns.zh: 是的。不，我认为迫使自己和团队以这种方式思考是一个非常好的思维训练，因为这能为你节省时间和金钱——如果你日后想对系统进行改动时，就不必不断重建，从而节省大量资金。这又回到了拥有清晰愿景和战略的重要性上。因为你正在进行的是长远规划。如今的决策都是为长远目标服务的。这样你就能朝着既定方向前进，而无需在每次想改变时都重新构建系统。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On the second order thinking, sorry, I called it second order decision, but in this framework that you spoke of, how do you actually operationalize this concept? When you're planning, do you write out in the document second order impact that we should be thinking about, or do you do something else?
turns.zh: 关于二阶思维，抱歉，我之前称之为二阶决策，但在你提到的这个框架中，如何将这个概念付诸实践呢？在规划阶段，你们是否会在文档中写明需要考虑的二阶影响，或者采取其他措施？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. So I think there's many ways to do this. If you have a spec-ed template or a piece of documentation that your team typically use when they're writing out product strategy or product requirements, et cetera, you can put a line in here to force people to think about it. I also think thinking about first principles and writing out first principles for the changes that you're making often are in service of second order thinking. Where it's like here are the things that we care about. Here's why these things are important. And we want to make sure these are baked into what we're building. Typically you'll write those through the lens of second order thinking. (00:45:36): Shopify uses first principles a lot in everything that they build. And this is something I took away from that way of working because it's extremely effective. If you can get teams to align on first principles early on, it saves you a lot of heartache later because you've got people to align way early days before you even got into the design process, or before you had to start thinking about how do we actually technically implement this. (00:45:56): And then the other way I would say is there's ways to structure or have thoughtful discussion around second order effects. That could be a brainstorm. You could use Miro to think about that. We're going to make these changes today. How do they cascade through our ecosystem? What are the gotchas or the things we need to worry about? And again, I think the more complex your ecosystem is, the more you are forced to do this. A lot of founders in early stage products don't think like this because they're so focused on the product market fit. We need to just get something that people are using. That then when they get product market fit, they realize when they get into scale mode, they didn't build something scalable, and they have to rebuild things which can actually really hurt them when they're trying to grow really quickly later on.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为有许多方法可以做到这一点。如果你有标准化的模板或文档，团队通常在制定产品策略或产品需求时使用，你可以在其中添加一行，强制人们思考这个问题。我还认为思考第一性原理，并为你正在进行的变更写下第一性原理，往往有助于二阶思维。比如，这里是我们关心的要点。这里是这些要点为何重要。我们要确保这些要点融入我们正在构建的产品中。通常，你会从二阶思维的角度来撰写这些内容。（00:45:36）：Shopify在开发的所有产品中都大量运用第一性原理。这是我从他们的工作方式中学到的，因为它非常有效。如果你能让团队早期就围绕第一性原理达成一致，日后就能省去很多麻烦，因为人们在设计过程开始前很久，甚至在你需要开始考虑如何在技术上实现这一功能之前，就已经达成了共识。（00:45:56）：另外，我想说还有一种方法，那就是围绕二阶影响进行结构化或深入讨论。这可以是一次头脑风暴。你可以使用Miro来思考这个问题。我们今天要进行这些变更。它们将如何在我们的生态系统中产生连锁反应？有哪些潜在问题或需要关注的方面？再说一次，我认为你的生态系统越复杂，就越需要这样做。许多早期产品创始人没有这样思考，因为他们过于专注于产品与市场的契合度。我们需要先开发出人们会使用的产品。但当他们实现产品与市场的契合后，却意识到当进入规模化阶段时，他们并没有构建出可扩展的产品，最终不得不重建，这在他们试图快速增长时会带来巨大阻碍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Absolutely. Happens all the time. For principles, do you put those in to say the team strategy, like the quarterly strategy document? Like here's our principles for the quarter? Is that how you generally do that?
turns.zh: 是啊，当然了。这种情况经常发生。关于原则部分，你们会把它们写进团队战略文件里吗？比如季度战略文档？会把我们的原则列在季度目标里吗？你们通常是这么操作的吗？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. I think that is a great place to put it. You can write them on the feature level too. So something that you're building, just getting clearer on here are the things that matter to us. Here's what we care about. We're going to design in service of these things. And here are the things that aren't that important. And again, those are the types of places in a product requirements doc where people will argue the most, which is a good thing because you're basically discussing and debating sort of foundations of what you're going to build before you get into the work of building it. And so those exercises are always a good idea.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得这地方放原则很合适。你也可以在功能层面写下这些原则。比如你正在开发的某个功能，就可以明确说明哪些是我们最重视的，哪些是我们关心的，我们要围绕这些核心设计。哪些又不是那么重要的。在产品需求文档中，这些部分往往是争论最激烈的地方，但这其实是件好事，因为在真正开始开发之前，你先把基础的东西反复讨论清楚。这种讨论永远都是有益的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I love that. Okay. So going back, because I wanted to close this thread, you've come up with your vision, your mission, your strategy, your goals as a team. People start to align around it. What do you do to kick it off and get people on board and aware of the plan, and then to stay on plan with that strategy and not kind of be distracted by new priorities and shiny objects?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我很赞同。好的，回到正题，因为我想结束这个话题。你们已经确定了团队的愿景、使命、战略和目标，团队成员也开始围绕这些理念达成共识。那么，你们是如何启动这个过程，让大家都参与进来、了解计划，并始终坚持执行既定战略，不被新任务或诱人项目分心呢？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yes. Oh, the shiny object thing is very real. Good question. So for example, I just did this recently where I brought my team along through the OKR process for Q2 planning. They had a say in basically what we decided we were going to work on. It went up for leadership approval. We got approval. And my process was I used Loom, which is another one of my favorite products. It's just a really easy screen share and video recording tool that you can share with teams. And so I just recapped, "All right, here's what I presented to leadership. Here are the feedback that we got. Here's the strategic feedback that we got. And here are the changes we're going to make. Any questions, let me know." And I posted it in Slack. (00:48:10): So I was just trying to keep the feedback loop really quick and tight with teams rather than wait till the next meeting you have with them a week later. I was like, all right, I'm going to just try to spend five minutes recording this and get it out ASAP. And that helps because then it gets people excited. Okay, cool. This thing that I worked on got really great feedback from leadership, and now we're working on it. I'm excited to get going. (00:48:29): And then it depends. Usually depending on the project, I have some sort of kickoff. I don't usually do a quarterly kickoff or anything like that because I think there's usually disparate teams owning different parts of strategy. But usually having a good weekly team meeting where you're really thoughtful about cascading feedback down from leadership, constantly checking in on what are we trying to do here? What is our strategy? How are these goals that we set laddering up? Are we achieving it? Are we not? Whatever. Having a meeting like that where you're kind of constantly talking about it each week also helps people feel bought in and not get distracted. (00:48:59): And actually I found that teams who are very bought to your vision and strategy are less distractable. Where I usually have more trouble is with leadership that aren't necessarily in the weeds with your team every day. And I'll get an idea. "Have you thought about doing this one random obscure thing?" "Yes. However, it's not in service of this long term plan, so we don't want to do that right now because we don't think it's the best use of our time."
turns.zh:
是的。哦，所谓的“闪亮物件”效应确实存在。这是个好问题。举个例子，我最近就让团队参与了第二季度规划的OKR流程。他们能对我们决定着手的项目提出意见。方案提交给领导层审批后，获得了批准。我的做法是使用Loom（我最喜欢的工具之一）——这是一个非常易用的屏幕共享和视频录制工具，可以与团队实时分享。之后我会总结道：“好的，以下是我向领导层汇报的内容。我们收到了哪些反馈？哪些是战略层面的反馈？接下来要做哪些调整？有任何问题随时提问。”然后我把这些内容发布到Slack上。

（00:48:10）：我之所以这样做，是为了让反馈循环尽可能快且紧密，而不是等到一周后再开会汇报。我会花五分钟录制视频并尽快发布，这样能激发大家的积极性。比如，我提出的某个项目得到了领导层的高度认可，现在我们正在推进这个项目。我很兴奋能开始行动了。

（00:48:29）：接下来要看具体项目情况。我通常不会举办季度启动会，因为不同团队负责不同的战略部分。但每周召开高效的团队会议很重要，要认真思考如何将领导层的反馈层层传递下去，不断核对我们的战略目标、进展和成效。这种每周持续沟通的方式能让团队成员更有归属感，也不容易分心。

（00:48:59）：我发现，那些对愿景和战略高度认同的团队更不容易被分心。而我更常遇到的问题是，领导层并非每天与团队深度沟通。比如我会提议：“有没有想过做这个奇特的功能？”对方回答：“有。但这不符合长期战略，所以我们现在不考虑这个方案。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. And the way you're describing it, this is as a manager of product managers-
turns.zh: 明白了。从你的描述来看，你是产品经理的管理者——

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... versus an ICPM? Cool. So as an ICPM, I imagine you would do a quarterly kickoff, or whatever your cycle length. You kick off with the team. Here's what we're doing. Any questions?
turns.zh: ……和ICPM相比呢？不错。作为ICPM，我想你会每季度召开启动会，或者根据周期调整。先和团队沟通：“我们要做这些事。有什么问题吗？”

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Another thing I wanted to make sure we have time to chat about is product review meetings and process. Just kind of like how do you, as a product leader, make sure that you're shipping great stuff that you're proud of and that your leaders aren't surprised by? How do you design just a product review and design process.
turns.zh: 好的。还有个我想聊聊的话题是产品评审会议和流程。作为产品负责人，如何确保交付的成果既出色又让领导层满意，不出乎他们的意料？如何设计产品评审和设计流程？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. So I have a lot of strong feelings on product reviews. And it's because I've been in a lot of different organizations and I've seen a lot of bad ways of doing this honestly. And I think it also depends on the product that you're building and the team that you've created. So I don't think that there's one right or wrong way to do this. (00:50:12): Where I've seen them fail is when they happen at the function level, and they're not done or shared as a team. Typically it's normal to have a design review or to have some sort of technical review. And the more you can try to bring those different review processes into one central moment to check in, the better it tends to go. Because what happens is you'll have feedback in a vacuum. The design leader will give the designer feedback, and then you don't hear about it. Or there'll be some technical flaw that happens in a very specific technical review that doesn't get back to the larger team. (00:50:43): So finding ways to make sure that those parts of your process are shared across each function, and you attend them and prepare for them as a team, I think really helps a lot of that. I'm not saying that you shouldn't have a design review. Of course you should. I mean, you should just be really thoughtful about having moments, especially if there are moments where you're blessing something to move forward, to making sure the whole team is there. And that there's a very strategic check-in process to get those things approved that everyone knows about and is a part of.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我对产品评审有很多强烈的看法。这是因为我曾在许多不同的组织中工作过，坦白说，我见过很多做得不好的方法。我认为这也取决于你正在开发的产品以及你组建的团队。因此，我不认为有一种正确或错误的做法。（00:50:12）：我见过他们失败的地方在于，这些评审发生在职能层面，而不是作为一个团队共同完成的。通常，进行设计评审或技术评审是正常的。如果你能尽可能将这些不同的评审过程整合到一个核心时刻进行检查，效果往往会更好。因为当反馈在真空中进行时，设计负责人会给设计师反馈，但其他人却听不到。或者在某次特定技术评审中发现的技术缺陷，也无法传达给整个团队。（00:50:43）：因此，确保这些流程环节在各职能部门之间共享，并让团队共同参与和准备，我认为这对改进非常有帮助。我并不是说你不应该进行设计评审。当然应该进行。但你需要认真考虑这些时刻，特别是当你要批准某个产品上线或构建时，要确保整个团队都参与其中。并建立一个战略性的检查流程，让每个人都了解并参与到这些获批事项中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is that a meeting that you do weekly and you invite the designer and the engineer? Who do you invite, I guess, and what is the goal of that meeting? The goal of that meeting, I imagine, is approved the product to go launch and build.
turns.zh: 那是一周一次的会议吗？你会邀请设计师和工程师吗？我猜你会邀请谁呢？这个会议的目标是什么？我想象，这个会议的目标是批准产品上线和构建。

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. And I think especially going back to the one way, two way door moment, giving teams autonomy to ship some things that you think are two way doors and aren't necessarily mission critical are important to your vision, but aren't going to conflate with the larger system, I think trying to keep things quick and not have too many barriers for people to ship is incredibly important. So you'll have to figure that out for your own org and it's nuances, but that is something that is important. (00:51:49): But when there are moments where you think it is basically a feedback gate, where it's a gate you need to walk through and a specific moment in time where you've gotten feedback, I think having a cross-functional meeting where there's a clear pre-read or something that's sent before. It's like, here's what we're talking about today. And then aligning on, do we think this meets our goals and does this meet our quality bar? And doing that in a really thoughtful way just so the team gets feedback. So the leadership is plugged in, but also so you're not standing the way of people shipping their products.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为特别是回到那个单向、双向的决策时刻，让团队有自主权去发布一些你认为是双向决策但不一定是关键任务的产品，对你的愿景很重要，但又不会与大系统冲突。我认为让事情快速推进，减少人们发布产品的障碍非常重要。因此，你需要根据自己的组织和其中的细微差别来调整，但这确实很重要。（00:51:49）：但当有些时候你认为这基本上是一个反馈关卡，一个你必须通过的关卡，在某个特定时间点获得反馈后，我认为召开跨职能会议非常重要。会议前要提前分发相关材料。比如，今天我们要讨论这些内容。然后达成一致意见：我们认为这是否符合我们的目标，是否达到了我们的质量标准？以一种深思熟虑的方式来做这件事，让团队获得反馈。这样一来，领导层也能参与其中，也不会阻碍人们发布他们的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then do you check in throughout the process of the product being built, or do you kind of encourage teams to get to a point where it's basically ready for approval?
turns.zh: 然后在产品构建过程中，你们会持续检查吗？还是说你们会鼓励团队在产品基本准备好等待批准时再行动？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. Ideally in a perfect world, there's three check-in moments. There is the first principles check-in. What are you trying to build, or what are you trying to do? What are the sort of foundations that you're going to build on? What is the most important thing? What are you solving for? Getting approval on that, weirdly, is almost the most important thing. Because it saves a lot of teams a lot of time when they get later in their feedback review process and people are like, "You're not solving for the right thing." So that's important. (00:52:49): Once you've aligned on that, then it's like, all right, what approach are we going to use? What are we going to build? And that's sort of how we solve the problem. Making sure that there is a technical component there too so there's some sort of infrastructure review or architecture review, or whatever you want to call it. And then it's like, all right, this is ready to ship. Let's check in again. Do we think it's ready? And I think that, again, it depends on your organization. If you have a very small team, you might be very plugged in and these things might not need to happen. But in bigger organizations, especially where leadership isn't always able to be in the room, making sure that you have a clear checking in a few times to make sure that everyone is moving in the right direction and everyone feels good is, I think, a worthwhile exercise.
turns.zh: 是的。理想情况下，如果一切顺利，应该有三个检查点：首先是基本原则检查。你们想构建什么，或者想做什么？你们将依托哪些基础？最重要的是什么？你们要解决什么问题？奇怪的是，获得对此的认可几乎是最重要的。因为当反馈审查过程进行到后期，团队可能会发现“你们解决的问题方向不对”，这会浪费大量时间。因此，这一点至关重要。（00:52:49）一旦大家达成共识，就要考虑：我们要采用什么方法？要构建什么？然后就是如何解决问题。同时也要确保有技术层面的审查，比如基础设施审查或架构审查。最后，再检查一遍：我们是否准备好上线了？我认为，这取决于你的组织规模。如果团队很小，大家可能沟通顺畅，流程可以省略。但在大型组织中，尤其是在领导层无法全程参与的情况下，多次清晰的检查点能确保大家方向正确、信心满满，这确实是值得采用的做法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Such a simple framework. And then one last question along those lines, do you leave it up to the team to schedule these meetings, or are you pulling it out of them and making sure they schedule it?
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这个框架。还有最后一个相关问题：你们是让团队自行安排这些会议，还是由管理层强制安排？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Today, because the team that I'm working on is pretty small, and we're pretty pre-product market fit, we're not doing a ton of very formal check-in moments because we don't need to be. Because it's a small team and we're all cruising together. But in bigger orgs that I've worked in, for Shopify, for example, there was a process around having these meetings and who would be there. And so those would kind of be scheduled through the larger processor system that they were working in, which really worked for them actually. And I think it allowed teams to be pretty autonomous on the day to day, but just making sure that there was feedback coming of from their users as well as from leadership.
turns.zh: 目前，我所在的团队规模较小，产品尚未真正面向市场，所以不需要太多的正式检查环节，因为团队沟通顺畅。但在大型组织中，比如Shopify，他们有严格的会议流程和参与人员规定。这些会议通常通过公司的大型流程系统进行安排，效果确实不错。这能让团队保持日常自主性，同时确保能及时获得用户和管理层的反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. One last question before we get to our exciting lightning round. And it's something that I've been thinking a lot about recently, which is around remote work as a product manager. I left Airbnb before COVID, and so I never lived in this world of everything is remote and product managing remotely. Is there anything you've picked up or learned that has been really helpful to being a product leader in a remote world?
turns.zh: 明白了。在进入精彩的闪电问答环节之前，最后再问一个问题。这是我最近思考很多的问题——远程工作的产品经理角色。新冠疫情前我就离开了Airbnb，所以从未经历过完全远程办公和远程产品管理的环境。你们有没有学到什么特别有用的经验，帮助你们在远程环境中担任产品领导者？

turns.speaker: Nickey Skarstad
turns.en: Yeah. I would say last couple years have just been a huge shift in my ways of working. I sort of grew up as a PM in IRL environments where we did the majority of our work together in the same room. So that was whiteboarding, having a quick sync after you had an in person meeting to finalize some details or keep hashing out a problem. It's so cheesy and overhyped, but the proverbial water cooler moment where you see somebody, and you're like, "Hey, how are you doing, Hey, did you hear about this thing?" All of those things literally went away overnight. (00:55:01): And I think especially the job of a PM, it's hard under normal times because you are doing so much labor to make sure people are informed and give feedback, et cetera. And then overnight you took away a lot of the methods that they were using to do it. And so I think that has been a pretty profound shift for a lot of people working in product roles. (00:55:21): The good news is there's a ton of new tools and new technology that's actually being built right now that's majorly helpful for this. So I use Slack in very new ways today than I did two years ago. Things like just making sure to post more asynchronous updates. Trying to actually take the burden off of an IRL or a Zoom meeting. Can we talk about this asynchronously and do it in Slack? Slack has this really great feature called huddles where you can just quickly get on. It's just audio. So there's no video. And you can just have a 30 second conversation. It's good for standups and things like that. Suggest you try it if you haven't yet. (00:55:56): And then a lot of the old in person whiteboarding, things like that, you can do those now using awesome tools like Miro and FigJam. And I feel like, especially at Airbnb, we had such an international team that there was always somebody who was remote typically. And I think we never really got the remote experience right. And now that the majority of our teams are remote, I'm a fully remote person, I've been a lot more thoughtful about making sure we're creating a really good experience of how we're working for the larger team. And so I think you have to hack on this with your team. Different teams have different ways of working, but trying to be a synchronous, using Slack, making sure you're following up in very visible ways where people can see. Don't rely on Zoom meetings to fill all of your time. Otherwise people will literally hate you. And things like that really make a huge difference.
turns.zh:
是的。过去这几年，我的工作方式发生了巨大转变。我最初在现实环境中担任产品经理时，我们大多在同一间会议室里共同完成大部分工作。比如白板头脑风暴、面对面会议后快速同步进展、持续解决问题等。这些看似老生常谈却实用的交流场景，如今却一夜之间消失了。（00:55:01）尤其对于产品经理来说，正常工作环境下就已经面临诸多挑战——要确保团队成员充分了解信息、收集反馈等等。然而疫情一来，很多传统沟通方式被迫消失。这对许多产品从业者来说无疑是巨大的转变。

（00:55:21）不过好消息是，目前涌现了大量新工具和新技术，能有效填补空白。比如我现在使用Slack的方式与两年前大不相同——更频繁地发布异步更新，减少面对面或Zoom会议的负担。Slack的Huddles功能特别实用，仅需语音通话，无需视频，30秒快速沟通，非常适合站立会议等场景。建议还没试过的朋友可以体验一下。

（00:55:56）还有很多传统的面对面白板协作场景，现在可以借助Miro、FigJam等优秀工具实现。比如在Airbnb，我们曾拥有国际化团队，总有成员处于远程状态，但始终未能优化远程体验。如今团队基本实现远程办公，我也开始更深入思考如何为整个团队打造优质的协作体验。这需要团队共同探索，针对不同团队特性灵活调整，比如通过Slack保持信息可见，避免过度依赖Zoom会议，否则只会招人厌烦。

turns.zh: 太棒了。非常有帮助。好的，尼基，你准备好参加闪电问答了吗？

And follow people that are not just tech people on Twitter. You are doing yourself a disservice if your entire feed is tech people. So find people that are plugged into cultural zeitgeist because it helps you also understand the moment in which you are shipping, and it'll make sure that you're acing your product marketing and your messaging and you're building the right thing.
turns.zh: 对，我超爱安妮·海伦·彼得森。她是一位文化记者，深度洞察时代文化脉动。当有人问我对新晋产品经理的首要建议时，我总是说要多做消费者。下载新产品，试用体验，这能让你成为更出色的产品打造者。此外，别只关注科技领域的人——如果你的信息流全是科技类内容，那就太局限了。所以，多关注文化潮流的引领者吧，这样能助你理解所处时代的脉搏，确保产品营销和信息传递精准无误，最终打造出正确的产品。
